# FEOD Full Context

> Expanded AI-readable context for FEOD (Fractal Entity Oriented Design), a frontend architecture methodology for modules, public API, fractal structure, and controlled dependencies.

Canonical site: https://fractal-oriented.tech/

English docs: https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/

Russian docs: https://fractal-oriented.tech/

## What FEOD Is

FEOD means Fractal Entity Oriented Design. It is a methodology for organizing frontend applications around structural entities with clear roles. The main goal is to keep a growing frontend codebase understandable, reviewable, and enforceable through import rules and explicit public APIs.

FEOD is not a UI component taxonomy and not a backend runtime module system. It is a source-code architecture model for frontend projects.

## Where To Start

Use these pages first:

- English overview: https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/get-started/overview
- Russian overview: https://fractal-oriented.tech/get-started/overview
- English quick start: https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/get-started/quick-start
- Russian quick start: https://fractal-oriented.tech/get-started/quick-start
- English FEOD in 5 minutes: https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/get-started/feod-in-5-minutes
- Russian FEOD in 5 minutes: https://fractal-oriented.tech/get-started/feod-in-5-minutes

For a new project, start with the minimal top-level structure and add modules only when a real responsibility exists. For an existing project, identify stable product areas first, then move imports behind public APIs gradually.

## Core Model

FEOD uses five canonical top-level levels:

- `app`: application startup, routing, providers, top-level composition, and application wiring.
- `pages`: route-level pages and large entry scenarios.
- `modules`: product or responsibility modules with internal structure and explicit public API.
- `common`: reusable FEOD entities not tied to one product module.
- `global`: environment declarations, shims, polyfills, and rare side-effect setup that affects the whole application.

The methodology treats files and directories as FEOD entities. A FEOD entity is a structural unit with a role and constraints. It is not the same as a DDD entity.

## Import Rules

The import matrix is the normative source for dependencies:

- `app` may compose pages, modules, and common entities.
- `pages` may use modules and common entities.
- `modules` may use common entities and their own internals.
- `common` must stay independent from product modules and pages.
- `global` must not become an application dependency bucket.

External code must not import internal files of another FEOD entity. Deep imports are treated as boundary violations because they turn implementation details into hidden public contracts.

Primary reference:

- https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/reference/import-matrix
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/reference/import-matrix

## Public API

Public API is the supported external contract of a FEOD entity. In TypeScript projects, it is usually represented by an `index.ts` file at the root of the entity.

Rules:

- consumers import another FEOD entity from its root public API;
- internal directories such as `ui`, `model`, `api`, `lib`, `config`, and `types` are not external entry points by default;
- an exported symbol becomes part of the supported contract;
- moving implementation files should not force consumers to update imports if the public API remains stable.

Primary reference:

- https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/reference/public-api
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/reference/public-api

## Fractality

Fractality means that the same structural discipline can repeat at different scales. A large module can contain internal submodules, and those submodules can also have roles and public APIs when the responsibility justifies it.

Fractality does not mean unlimited nesting. A new level or submodule should appear only when it reduces ambiguity and protects a real boundary.

Primary reference:

- https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/core-concepts/fractality
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/core-concepts/fractality

## Entity Orientation

Entity orientation means every structural element should have a clear role. When a developer sees `app`, `pages`, `modules`, `common`, `global`, `index.ts`, or a module README, they should understand what belongs there and what does not.

FEOD entity is a documentation and structure term. Do not explain it as a DDD entity unless explicitly contrasting the two.

Primary reference:

- https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/core-concepts/entity-orientation
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/core-concepts/entity-orientation

## Common Boundaries

`common` is not a dumping ground. It stores reusable FEOD entities that are not tied to one product module. If code knows a specific business scenario, it usually belongs in a module, not in `common`.

Use `common` for stable technical contracts and shared entities with clear reuse criteria. Avoid moving code there only because two places currently need it.

Primary guide:

- https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/guides/common-boundaries
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/guides/common-boundaries

## Migration Notes

When migrating from FSD, FEOD should not be treated as a mechanical rename of layers. FEOD uses levels and modules, not FSD layers, slices, and segments as the primary structure.

When migrating from regular modular architecture, the main work is usually to define public APIs, stop deep imports, and make dependency direction explicit.

Useful guides:

- https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/guides/migration-from-fsd
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/guides/migration-from-modular
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/guides/migration-from-fsd
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/guides/migration-from-modular

## Review Checklist

When reviewing FEOD changes, check:

- whether the new code belongs to the chosen level;
- whether module boundaries are explicit;
- whether external imports go through public API;
- whether `common` contains only independent reusable entities;
- whether deep imports introduce hidden coupling;
- whether exceptions are documented instead of becoming implicit rules.

Primary guide:

- https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/guides/code-review
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/guides/code-review

## Tools

FEOD documentation describes future and supporting tool scenarios:

- FEOD Analyzer: graph, import, and public API checks.
- ESLint plugin: lint rules for accepted architecture constraints.
- AI rules: project instructions for AI-assisted work.
- FEOD config: machine-readable configuration for levels, modules, and allowed deviations.

Tool pages:

- https://fractal-oriented.tech/en/tools/
- https://fractal-oriented.tech/tools/

## Canonical Terms

Use these terms consistently:

- FEOD
- Fractal Entity Oriented Design
- FEOD entity
- level
- module
- public API
- import matrix
- deep import
- controlled dependency

Avoid presenting FEOD as a renamed FSD, a universal backend architecture, or a UI component methodology.
